TIME CLOCK ROUNDING PRACTICES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this Time Clock Rounding information sheet to describe how California law treats the practice of rounding an hourly employee's recorded time punches — such as Jordan Lee's — to the nearest preset increment (for example, the nearest five or ten minutes) for wage-calculation purposes. California courts have addressed this practice differently depending on what the rounded time is being used to calculate: general work-time calculations (used to compute regular and overtime wages) are treated under one standard, while time punches used to determine compliance with meal period timing requirements are treated under a different, more exacting standard. This document describes both.

WHAT ROUNDING IS, AND THE MEAL PERIOD HOLDING
The California Supreme Court in Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC described the practice of rounding time punches as "adjusting the hours that an employee has actually worked to the nearest preset time increment." Addressing whether that practice may be applied to the time punches employers use to determine whether a meal period met the timing requirements of Labor Code section 512 and the applicable wage order, the Court held that it may not: employers cannot round time punches in the meal period context, because the meal period provisions are designed to prevent even minor infringements on meal period requirements, and rounding is incompatible with that objective.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "we hold that employers cannot engage in the practice of rounding time punches — that is, adjusting the hours that an employee has actually worked to the nearest preset time increment — in the meal period context. The meal period provisions are designed to prevent even minor infringements on meal period requirements, and rounding is incompatible with that objective."
  — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal. 5th 58 (Cal. 2021) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4859143/donohue-v-amn-services-llc/)
  Known gap: This clause states a specific, narrow holding of Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC: rounding of time punches is not permitted when those punches are being used to determine meal period compliance. It does not state a general prohibition on all forms of time rounding for all purposes; the separate clauses below address the different standard that applies when rounded time is used only to calculate regular and overtime wages, and this document's scope-limitation clause addresses what Donohue did and did not decide about that separate standard.

THE FEDERAL "ROUNDING" REGULATION CALIFORNIA COURTS HAVE LOOKED TO
For time rounding used to calculate regular and overtime wages generally (as opposed to rounding applied to meal period timing), California courts have looked for guidance to a federal Fair Labor Standards Act regulation on "rounding" practices, 29 C.F.R. section 785.48(b), which describes the longstanding industry practice of recording start and stop times to the nearest five minutes, tenth of an hour, or quarter hour, and states the federal enforcement standard for it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "It has been found that in some industries, particularly where time clocks are used, there has been the practice for many years of recording the employees' starting time and stopping time to the nearest 5 minutes, or to the nearest one-tenth or quarter of an hour. Presumably, this arrangement averages out so that the employees are fully compensated for all the time they actually work. For enforcement purposes this practice of computing working time will be accepted, provided that it is used in such a manner that it will not result, over a period of time, in failure to compensate the employees properly for all the time they have actually worked."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 785.48(b) — "Rounding" Practices (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations), 29 C.F.R. § 785.48(b) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-B/part-785/subpart-D/section-785.48)
  Known gap: This is a federal Department of Labor regulation, not a California statute. It is quoted here because California courts (see the See's Candy Shops clause below) have adopted its standard as the measure of when a rounding policy is lawful under California wage law, not because the regulation itself independently governs California employers under state law.

SEE'S CANDY SHOPS: THE CALIFORNIA STANDARD FOR ROUNDING REGULAR AND OVERTIME WAGES
The California Court of Appeal in See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court adopted the federal rounding regulation's standard as the rule under California law for calculating regular and overtime wages: an employer may use a rounding policy — the court's case involved a nearest-tenth-of-an-hour policy — if the policy is fair and neutral on its face and is used in a manner that will not result, over time, in a failure to compensate employees properly for all the time they have actually worked. The court explained that, assuming a rounding-over-time policy is neutral both facially and as applied, the practice is proper under California law because its net effect is to permit employers to efficiently calculate hours worked without imposing any burden on employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "we have concluded that the rule in California is that an employer is entitled to use the nearest-tenth rounding policy if the rounding policy is fair and neutral on its face and “it is used in such a manner that it will not result, over a period of time, in failure to compensate the employees properly for all the time they have actually worked.”"
  — See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court, 210 Cal. App. 4th 889, 907 (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist., Div. 1, 2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811430/sees-candy-shops-inc-v-superior-court/)
  "Assuming a rounding-over-time policy is neutral, both facially and as applied, the practice is proper under California law because its net effect is to permit employers to efficiently calculate hours worked without imposing any burden on employees."
  — See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court, 210 Cal. App. 4th 889, 903 (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist., Div. 1, 2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811430/sees-candy-shops-inc-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court is a California Court of Appeal decision, not a California Supreme Court decision. As the scope-limitation clause below explains, the California Supreme Court in Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC expressly noted it has never decided the validity of this standard and was not asked to do so in that case, even though Donohue proceeded to assume the standard's validity for purposes of deciding the separate meal-period question.

WHAT "NEUTRAL, OVER TIME" HAS BEEN HELD TO MEAN
Discussing the neutrality standard, the California Supreme Court in Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC recounted how federal courts interpreting the same federal regulation had described the line between a lawful and unlawful rounding policy: federal courts had interpreted the regulation to permit rounding policies as long as they, on average, favor neither overpayment nor underpayment, and rounding policies violate the regulation if they systematically undercompensate employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Federal courts had interpreted the regulation to permit rounding policies as long as they “on average, favor[] neither overpayment nor underpayment” and do not “ ‘consistently result[] in a failure to pay employees for time worked.’ ”"
  — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal. 5th 58 (Cal. 2021) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4859143/donohue-v-amn-services-llc/)
  "rounding policies violate the regulation if they “systematically undercompensate employees”"
  — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal. 5th 58 (Cal. 2021) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4859143/donohue-v-amn-services-llc/)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the California Supreme Court's own opinion in Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, which in turn is quoting and summarizing a federal district court decision, Alonzo v. Maximus, Inc. (C.D. Cal. 2011) 832 F.Supp.2d 1122. The Alonzo opinion itself was not independently fetched or verified for this clause; the quotes below are Donohue's own verified text describing that case's reasoning, not an independently confirmed quotation of Alonzo's opinion.

THE PRECISE MEAL PERIOD TIMING REQUIREMENTS ROUNDING WOULD DISRUPT
The meal period timing requirements that a rounding policy in the meal period context would affect are stated in specific, non-rounded terms. Labor Code section 512(a) requires a first meal period of not less than 30 minutes for a work period of more than five hours, and a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes for a work period of more than 10 hours (subject to waiver rules for shorter work periods). The applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order states the same 30-minute, five-hour threshold in nearly identical terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee. An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than 10 hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12 hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of the employer and the employee only if the first meal period was not waived."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 512(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=512.)
  "No employer shall employ any person for a work period of more than five (5) hours without a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that when a work period of not more than six (6) hours will complete the day’s work the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of the employer and the employee."
  — Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A) (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 8, § 11040), IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause quotes IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 11(A), which applies to employees in professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations; other wage orders govern other industries and occupations and may phrase their own meal period provisions somewhat differently, though the same 30-minute/five-hour structure is common across the wage orders addressed in Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court and Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC. This clause does not independently verify the meal period text of every other numbered wage order.

WHY THE COURT FOUND ROUNDING INCOMPATIBLE WITH MEAL PERIOD PRECISION
The Donohue court illustrated why rounding is incompatible with the meal period timing requirements using an example involving a rounding policy that rounds to the nearest 10-minute increment: an employee provided with a 21-minute lunch from 12:04 p.m. to 12:25 p.m. would have that lunch recorded, after rounding, as a 30-minute lunch from 12:00 p.m. to 12:30 p.m. — meaning the employee would have lost nine of the 30 minutes to which he or she was entitled, and the timekeeping system would not have flagged the lunch as a meal period violation at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Consider, for example, an employee who is provided with a 21-minute lunch from 12:04 p.m. to 12:25 p.m. Under AMN’s timekeeping system, which rounded time punches to the nearest 10-minute increment, the lunch would have been recorded as a 30-minute lunch from 12:00 p.m. to 12:30 p.m. In that scenario, an employee would have lost nine of the 30 minutes — or almost a third of the time — to which he or she was entitled, and Team Time would not have flagged the lunch as a meal period violation."
  — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal. 5th 58 (Cal. 2021) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4859143/donohue-v-amn-services-llc/)
  Known gap: This is the specific numeric example the Donohue court used to illustrate its reasoning; it describes AMN's own 10-minute rounding increment in that case, not a generalized claim that all rounding increments produce a nine-minute loss. A different rounding increment (for example, rounding to the nearest five minutes) would produce different, generally smaller, potential losses, though the court's underlying holding that meal-period time punches may not be rounded at all does not depend on the size of the increment used.

WHAT DONOHUE DID AND DID NOT DECIDE ABOUT GENERAL WAGE-ROUNDING
The California Supreme Court in Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC was explicit about the limits of what it decided. The Court stated that it has never decided the validity of the neutral-rounding standard articulated in See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court, and that it was not asked to do so in the Donohue case. The Court went on to hold that even assuming that standard's validity, a rounding policy applied in the meal period context does not comport with the standard's own neutrality requirement — meaning the meal-period holding does not depend on, and does not resolve, whether the See's Candy neutral-rounding standard is itself the correct rule for general wage calculations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "This court has never decided the validity of the rounding standard articulated in See’s Candy I, and we are not asked to do so here."
  — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal. 5th 58 (Cal. 2021) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4859143/donohue-v-amn-services-llc/)
  "But even assuming the validity of See’s Candy I, a rounding policy in the meal period context does not comport with its neutrality standard."
  — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal. 5th 58 (Cal. 2021) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4859143/donohue-v-amn-services-llc/)
  Known gap: This clause states the California Supreme Court's own description of what it left open. As a result, See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court remains Court of Appeal authority (not California Supreme Court authority) for the proposition that neutral rounding is permitted when calculating regular and overtime wages generally; whether the California Supreme Court would adopt that standard if squarely presented with the question has not been independently confirmed here and, per Donohue's own text, has not yet been decided by that Court.

SIGNATURE AND RECEIPT
